newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SA WEEK AHEAD - JANUARY TRADE SURPLUS SEEN HEALTHY.
newsitem.headline: SA WEEK AHEAD - JANUARY TRADE SURPLUS SEEN HEALTHY.

text.p: South Africa should have recorded another healthy trade surplus in January although economists are not expecting a repeat of December's bumper 2.04 billion rand.
The consensus of analysts polled by Reuters was for a 817 million rand surplus, with the range between 500 million and one billion rand.

Nick Barnardt of BOE NatWest said the hefty surpluses recorded at the end of 1996 had been distorted by the inclusion of previously-missed exports -- notably of gold -- and the fact that imports were traditionally low in the run-up to Christmas.
"The last few months of last year gave an artificial impression. Those figures were inflated by the inclusion of exports that weren't included earlier in the year."
"December was a bit of an exceptional month and we don't expect it to be like that every month," said an economist who declined to be identified.
Economists also noted that seasonal factors in January would also dent the figure.
"A lot of factories start a little bit late in January so one would expect a lower figure," said Francois Jansen, an economist with Boland Bank.

He also expected the rand's 29 percent depreciation against the dollar last year to begin having a positive effect on exports, pointing out that it took time for the effects of the currency depreciation to filter through.

"The exports will get a kickstart from the rand depreciation last year and also because the domestic economy is slowing down...manufacturers are looking at other ways to increase production and they are looking at exporting," Jansen said.

Economists said that while the rand had strengthened markedly against its major trading partners' currencies during January, it would have little impact on the trade balance in the current month, mainly as a result of time lags on trade contracts.
Herman van Papendorp, economist at SMK Securities, said he expected the rand to weaken to around 4.70 against the dollar by year-end, which would boost exports in the months ahead.
"I do think the depreciation of the rand, which will be slower than it was last year, and higher global growth will have a positive impact on exports," he said.
Economists expect an improved trade balance in 1997 to help reduce the current account deficit to between one and five billion rand this year.
While 1996's current account deficit has yet to be announced, Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals said last week that he expected it to be well below the 10 billion rand recorded in 1995.
January trade data is scheduled for release from Tuesday this week.
